opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the intervention experiments are what turn the work from storytelling into something closer to science.

When you build an attribution graph, you get a hypothesis about how the model is computing something. You see features light up, you see edges between them, and it's very tempting to read a clean narrative into that. But the graph is built on a replacement model, an approximation of the real thing, so there's always a question: is this what the model is actually doing, or just a plausible-looking artifact of our method?

Interventions let us check. If the graph says a certain feature is carrying an intermediate step, we can reach into the model, suppress that feature or swap in a different one, and see whether the output changes the way the graph predicts. The two-hop reasoning example is a nice illustration. If the model seems to go "Dallas, so Texas, so Austin," we can turn down the Texas representation, inject something like California instead, and watch the answer shift to Sacramento. When that works, you've learned something real about the mechanism rather than just a correlation.

The planning results in poetry were similar, and honestly one of the more surprising things for me. The graphs suggested the model was choosing a rhyme word before it started writing the line. When we intervened on that planned word, the model rewrote the whole line to land on the new target. That's hard to explain unless there really is some forward planning going on.

The other thing I value is that interventions keep us honest about where the method fails. Sometimes you intervene and nothing happens, or something unexpected happens, and that tells you the graph missed something, maybe an alternate pathway or error terms carrying a lot of weight. Those failures matter just as much, because they show us where our tools are still incomplete and where we shouldn't overclaim.

r001.rationale: The response values interventions for testing graph predictions and revealing mechanisms, but does not say that discovering how the model works is more valuable than using interventions to validate the graph.

r002.rationale: It says intervening on the planned rhyme word made the model rewrite the line to land on the new target.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that I find most valuable about the interventions is that they're really the part that turns the whole thing from a story into something you can actually check.

Because the way the method works, you train these replacement models, these cross-layer transcoders, and you get features out, and then you build an attribution graph for a given prompt that says, okay, here's how the model got from the input to the output, these are the features that fired and these are the ones that influenced each other. And when you look at those graphs, they're very compelling. You see a feature for, say, "Texas" and a feature for "capital" and then a feature for "say Austin," and it's a really nice narrative. But the graph is built on an approximation. The replacement model isn't the real model, there's error we're not accounting for, attention patterns are frozen, and so on. So the honest question is always: is this what's actually happening inside the model, or is this just a pretty picture we made up?

And the interventions are how you answer that. You go back to the real model, you take a feature that the graph says is important, you clamp it, you suppress it or you boost it or you swap it for a different one, and you look at what happens to the output. If I suppress the "Texas" feature and the model stops saying Austin and starts saying something else, now I actually have evidence the mechanism is real. And when it doesn't work, that's informative too, because it tells you the graph was misleading you somewhere.

The example I like a lot is the multi-step reasoning case, where the model has to do something like "the capital of the state containing Dallas." The graph suggests there's an intermediate "Texas" representation that the model never says out loud. And you can go in and swap that intermediate for, say, California, and the model says Sacramento. That's the kind of thing where the intervention isn't just confirming the picture, it's really demonstrating that the model is doing a genuine internal step that it's not verbalizing. Same with the poetry planning case, where you intervene on the rhyme-candidate features at the end of a line and the model rewrites the whole next line to land on the new word.

So for me that's the value. It's the thing that keeps us honest. Interpretability has a long history of methods that produce beautiful explanations that turn out not to be causal, and the interventions are the discipline that forces you to ask, every time, did I actually find a mechanism or did I just find a correlation that looks good on a diagram.

r001.rationale: The response presents interventions as the way to validate the graph and establish causal mechanisms; it does not say discovering how the model works is more valuable than that validation.

r002.rationale: It says intervening on rhyme-candidate features makes the model rewrite the next line to land on a new word, communicating that intervention changes its plan.

astra-6.text:
For me, the most valuable part is that interventions let us test whether our explanation actually predicts what the model does. You can look at a circuit and tell a plausible story about how information flows through it, but that alone doesn’t establish that the model is using the computation you’ve described.

Once you have that hypothesis, you can change something inside the model—suppress a feature, for example—and ask, “Does the downstream behavior change in the way we predicted?” That’s a much stronger test than simply observing that a feature activates on relevant inputs.

And the failures are useful, too. If an intervention doesn’t have the expected effect, that tells us our explanation is incomplete or wrong. So the exciting thing is being able to move from an interesting visualization to an explanation that makes testable predictions. It doesn’t mean we understand everything the model is doing, but it gives us a way to check whether we’re making progress.

r001.rationale: It frames interventions as a way to test whether the circuit explanation predicts model behavior, not discovering how the model works as more valuable than validating the graph.

r002.rationale: It gives suppressing a feature as an example but does not mention an identified planning direction or say that changing it changes the model’s plan.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most valuable thing is that they let us move from a plausible explanation to a testable prediction. We can look at a circuit and say, “We think this feature is influencing the answer through this path.” But then we can intervene—suppress that feature or change its activation—and see whether the model’s behavior changes in the way we predicted.

That’s a much stronger test than finding something that looks interpretable. And the failures are valuable too: if an intervention doesn’t do what we expect, that tells us our explanation is incomplete. So I see these experiments as a way to check whether we’re actually understanding the computation, rather than just telling a convincing story about it.

r001.rationale: The response says interventions help test explanations and understand computation, but does not present discovering how the model works as more valuable than validating the circuit-tracing graph.

r002.rationale: It describes intervening on a feature or its activation in general; it does not mention an identified planning direction or a resulting change in the model’s plan.
